kcet|Mathematics|2007|6|MTG Karnataka-CE:
The dot product needs the angle **between the two vectors as drawn from a common point**, so
the first task is to see which angle that is.
**Step 1 — read the vectors.** The question gives **OA** and **BO**, but asks for
**OA · OB**. Note that OB = −BO, so |OB| = |BO| = **6**, and |OA| = **5**.
**Step 2 — identify the angle.** Both OA and OB start at **O**, and the angle between them
is ∠AOB. The question states **∠BOA = 60°**, which is the same angle ✓
**Step 3 — apply the definition.**
OA · OB = |OA| |OB| cos(∠AOB)
= 5 × 6 × cos 60°
= 30 × ½
= **15** ✓
The care needed is over **BO versus OB**. The magnitude is the same either way, so the
magnitude 6 transfers directly; but had the question asked for **OA · BO**, the vector would
point the other way and the answer would be **−15** — which is option (c), placed there for
exactly that confusion.
Reading the direction of each arrow, and checking that both tails sit at the same point
before using the angle, is the whole of the care required.
Option (d), 15√3, would come from using sin 60° instead of cos 60°, that is from computing
the magnitude of the **cross** product rather than the dot product.
∴ 15.
kcet|Mathematics|2008|11|MTG Karnataka-C:
The **projection of ā on b̄** is the component of ā in the direction of b̄:
**projection = (ā · b̄) / |b̄|**
Note the denominator is the modulus of **b̄**, the vector projected *onto*.
**Step 1 — the dot product.** With ā = (3, −1, 5) and b̄ = (2, 3, 1):
ā · b̄ = (3)(2) + (−1)(3) + (5)(1)
= 6 − 3 + 5
= **8**
**Step 2 — the modulus of b̄.**
|b̄| = √(2² + 3² + 1²) = √(4 + 9 + 1) = **√14**
**Step 3 — divide.**
projection = **8/√14** ✓
The one thing to get right is **which modulus** goes in the denominator. Dividing by |ā| =
√(9 + 1 + 25) = √35 would give 8/√35 — option (c), and it answers the opposite question,
the projection of b̄ on ā.
The wording settles it: 'projection of ā **on** b̄' means the shadow ā casts along b̄, so b̄
supplies the direction and |b̄| the normalisation.
Option (b), √14, is the modulus of b̄ by itself, and option (d) uses √39, which is neither.
As a numerical check, 8/√14 ≈ 2·14, comfortably less than |ā| ≈ 5·92 — a projection can
never exceed the length of the vector being projected ✓
∴ 8/√14.
kcet|Mathematics|2011|21|MTG Karnataka-C:
Every term here is a **scalar triple product**, and the key fact is that all its cyclic
forms are **equal**.
**The identity.**
**ā·(b̄ × c̄) = b̄·(c̄ × ā) = c̄·(ā × b̄)**
Call this common value **[ā b̄ c̄]**. Because ā, b̄, c̄ are **non-coplanar**, it is non-zero —
which is what allows the divisions below.
**Step 1 — the first term.**
ā · {(b̄ × c̄) / [3 b̄·(c̄ × ā)]}
The denominator is a scalar, so it comes outside:
= [ā b̄ c̄] / (3[ā b̄ c̄])
= **1/3**
**Step 2 — the second term.**
b̄ · {(c̄ × ā) / [2 c̄·(ā × b̄)]}
= [ā b̄ c̄] / (2[ā b̄ c̄])
= **1/2**
**Step 3 — subtract.**
1/3 − 1/2 = 2/6 − 3/6 = **−1/6** ✓
Everything cancels because the three triple products are the **same number**, however the
letters are arranged — provided the order is **cyclic**. (A single swap, as in ā·(c̄ × b̄),
would change the sign.)
The non-coplanarity condition is not decoration: if the three were coplanar the triple
product would be zero and every fraction would be 0/0, undefined.
The answer is a pure number with no vectors in it, which is itself a sign that the triple
products were meant to cancel.
∴ −1/6.
kcet|Mathematics|2018|46|MTG Karnataka-C:
Two conditions give two equations in λ and μ.
**Condition 1 — orthogonal**, so the dot product is zero. With ā = (1, λ, 2) and
b̄ = (μ, 1, −1):
(1)(μ) + (λ)(1) + (2)(−1) = 0
μ + λ − 2 = 0
**λ + μ = 2**  … (i)
**Condition 2 — equal magnitudes**, so compare the squares:
|ā|² = 1 + λ² + 4 = **λ² + 5**
|b̄|² = μ² + 1 + 1 = **μ² + 2**
Setting them equal:
λ² + 5 = μ² + 2
**λ² − μ² = −3**  … (ii)
**Step 3 — factorise (ii).**
(λ − μ)(λ + μ) = −3
and substituting λ + μ = 2 from (i):
2(λ − μ) = −3
**λ − μ = −3/2**  … (iii)
**Step 4 — solve (i) and (iii) together.** Adding them:
2λ = 2 − 3/2 = 1/2 ⟹ **λ = 1/4**
and then from (i), **μ = 2 − 1/4 = 7/4**
So **(λ, μ) = (1/4, 7/4)** ✓
**Check both conditions:** dot product = 7/4 + 1/4 − 2 = 2 − 2 = **0** ✓ and
|ā|² = 1 + 1/16 + 4 = 81/16, |b̄|² = 49/16 + 2 = 81/16 ✓ equal.
Factorising the difference of squares is what makes the pair linear and quick to solve;
squaring and substituting directly would give a quadratic.
∴ (1/4, 7/4).
kcet|Mathematics|2004|48||0|0:
The **subnormal** at a point is
**subnormal = y · (dy/dx)**
so compute it for the curve and see what makes it independent of y.
**Step 1 — differentiate yⁿ = a^(n−1) x implicitly.**
n y^(n−1) (dy/dx) = a^(n−1)
**dy/dx = a^(n−1) / (n y^(n−1))**
**Step 2 — form the subnormal.**
y (dy/dx) = y × a^(n−1)/(n y^(n−1))
= (a^(n−1)/n) × y^(1 − (n−1))
= (a^(n−1)/n) · **y^(2 − n)**
**Step 3 — impose that it is constant.** Since a and n are constants, the subnormal depends
on the point only through **y^(2−n)**. For it to be the same at **every** point, that power
must vanish:
2 − n = 0
**n = 2** ✓
**Check:** with n = 2 the curve is y² = ax, a parabola, and the subnormal is a^(1)/2 = **a/2**
— a constant, independent of where on the curve you stand ✓
That is the well-known property of the parabola: **its subnormal is constant**, equal to
half the latus rectum. The question is really asking which member of the family yⁿ = a^(n−1)x
is a parabola, and the answer is n = 2.
The companion property, worth knowing alongside, is that the **subtangent of an exponential**
curve is constant.
∴ 2.
kcet|Mathematics|2004|51||0|0:
Parallel lines have **equal gradients**, so find the line's gradient and then the point where
the curve matches it.
**Step 1 — the gradient of the line.** Rearranging 4x − 2y − 1 = 0:
2y = 4x − 1
y = 2x − 1/2
**gradient = 2**
**Step 2 — the gradient of the curve.**
y = 6x − x²
**dy/dx = 6 − 2x**
**Step 3 — set them equal.**
6 − 2x = 2
2x = 4
**x = 2**
**Step 4 — find the y-coordinate from the curve.**
y = 6(2) − 2² = 12 − 4 = **8**
So the point of tangency is **(2, 8)** ✓
**Check:** the point lies on the curve ✓ and the gradient there is 6 − 4 = 2, matching the
line ✓
The second check is worth making in questions like this, because three of the four options
can be eliminated simply by testing whether they **lie on the curve** at all:
(8, 2): 6(8) − 64 = −16 ≠ 2 ✗
(6, −1): 36 − 36 = 0 ≠ −1 ✗
(4, 2): 24 − 16 = 8 ≠ 2 ✗
Only (2, 8) survives, without any differentiation — a useful shortcut when time is short.
∴ (2, 8).

kcet|Mathematics|2007|47||0|0.s:
The length of the **subtangent** at a point is
**subtangent = y / (dy/dx)**
**Step 1 — differentiate x²y² = a⁴ implicitly.** Using the product rule:
2xy² + x²(2y)(dy/dx) = 0
2x²y (dy/dx) = −2xy²
**dy/dx = −y/x**
**Step 2 — substitute into the formula.**
subtangent = y ÷ (−y/x)
= y × (x/−y)
= **−x**
**Step 3 — evaluate at the point (−a, a).**
subtangent = −(−a) = **a** ✓
The result is positive, as a length must be, and no modulus is needed because x is itself
negative at this point.
The curve is worth identifying: x²y² = a⁴ means **xy = ±a²**, a pair of rectangular
hyperbolas. For such a curve the subtangent at any point equals the x-coordinate in
magnitude — which is why the answer is simply a, with no factor of 2 or 1/2.
Taking logarithms is the quicker route to the gradient: 2 log x + 2 log y = 4 log a gives
1/x + (1/y)y′ = 0 and so y′ = −y/x in a single line.
∴ a.

Note: the printed key gives (2), a/2. The subtangent works out to −x, which at x = −a is a,
not a/2, so the key is wrong and has been corrected to (4).

kcet|Mathematics|2013|29|MTG Karnataka-C:
Expand the perpendicularity condition as a dot product and use ā ⊥ b̄ to kill the cross
terms.
**Step 1 — write the condition.** Two vectors are perpendicular when their dot product is
zero:
(ā + b̄) · (ā + m b̄) = 0
**Step 2 — expand.**
ā·ā + m(ā·b̄) + b̄·ā + m(b̄·b̄) = 0
**Step 3 — use ā ⊥ b̄.** That means **ā·b̄ = 0**, and also b̄·ā = 0, so both middle terms
vanish:
|ā|² + m|b̄|² = 0
**Step 4 — solve for m.**
m|b̄|² = −|ā|²
**m = −|ā|²/|b̄|²** ✓
The **minus sign** is forced: |ā|² and |b̄|² are both positive, so m must be negative — which
alone eliminates option (b), 1, and option (d), 0.
Option (a), −1, would be right only in the special case **|ā| = |b̄|**, and nothing in the
question says the two have equal length. Recognising that the answer must depend on the
magnitudes is the point of the question.
A geometric reading: with ā ⊥ b̄ the two vectors are the sides of a rectangle, and the
condition says the diagonal ā + b̄ is perpendicular to ā + mb̄. That happens exactly when the
second vector is the other diagonal of a suitably scaled rectangle, which fixes m as the
negative ratio of the squared lengths.
∴ −|ā|²/|b̄|².
kcet|Mathematics|2013|29||0|0:
If **ā is perpendicular to both b̄ and c̄**, it points along the **common normal** to those two
vectors.
**Step 1 — identify that direction.** The cross product **b̄ × c̄** is by definition
perpendicular to both b̄ and c̄, so it also lies along the common normal. Therefore
**ā is parallel to (b̄ × c̄)**
**Step 2 — use the property of the cross product.** For two **parallel** vectors the cross
product vanishes, since |ū × v̄| = |ū||v̄| sin θ and θ = 0:
**ā × (b̄ × c̄) = 0̄** ✓
Why the others fail:
**ā · (b̄ × c̄) = 0** ✗ — this is the **scalar triple product**, which vanishes when the three
vectors are **coplanar**. Here ā is perpendicular to the plane of b̄ and c̄, so the triple
product is at its largest, not zero. (It also equals the volume of the box they span, which
is plainly non-zero.)
**ā × (b̄ + c̄) = 0̄** ✗ — the sum b̄ + c̄ lies **in** the plane of b̄ and c̄, so it is
perpendicular to ā and their cross product has **maximum** magnitude.
**ā + (b̄ + c̄) = 0̄** ✗ — nothing in the hypothesis constrains the magnitudes, so the sum need
not vanish.
The distinction being tested is between the **vector** triple product, which is zero when ā
is along the normal, and the **scalar** triple product, which is zero when ā lies in the
plane — opposite conditions, and easy to confuse.
∴ ā × (b̄ × c̄) = 0̄.
